text: Lesson 9 shrank network policy down to a single workload instead of a whole subnet. This lesson takes that same move and applies it to remote access itself — the thing a VPN has handled for decades, and the thing that turns out to violate least privilege in almost exactly the same way a flat network does.

Here's what a traditional VPN actually grants. A user authenticates once, at connection time. Their device then joins the corporate network with a routable IP, sitting alongside everything else on it. From that point forward, the VPN's job is done — whatever the network itself permits is what the user can reach. A contractor who needs one internal app almost always ends up with reachability to a lot more than that one app, simply because that's how the network happens to be wired.

A software-defined perimeter inverts that. Identity and device posture get evaluated first, before any connection opens — and if that check fails, the application doesn't just deny the request, it doesn't respond at all. To anyone unauthorized scanning for it, a properly cloaked application looks like it isn't there. Only once a request is actually authorized does a connection open, and even then it's scoped to that one application, not the network around it.

Zero Trust Network Access products implement this through a broker and a connector. A lightweight connector sits inside the private network, right next to the application, and makes an outbound-only connection out to a cloud broker — no inbound firewall port ever has to open for it. When a user requests access, the broker checks their identity and device compliance, then stitches together one connection, scoped to that one app. Zscaler Private Access, Cloudflare Access, and Microsoft Entra Private Access are three real products built on exactly this pattern.

The user's device never gets a routable IP on that private network and never sees anything else it hosts — which is the whole point. It's the same shrinking Lesson 9 did for workload-to-workload traffic, now applied to a human's remote session. Next lesson turns to a different kind of least privilege: taking the just-in-time access and PAM patterns you already know from one team's Entra tenant, and applying them across an entire enterprise.
